nodes.title: Bhīṣma
nodes.summary: Śāntanu’s son and the Kuru elder. He gives up the throne, commands Duryodhana’s forces, then teaches Yudhiṣṭhira.

nodes.title: Draupadī
nodes.summary: Drupada’s daughter and wife of the five Pāṇḍavas. She challenges the assembly’s authority and shares exile with the brothers.

nodes.title: Yudhiṣṭhira
nodes.summary: The eldest Pāṇḍava. He loses his kingdom at dice, becomes king after the war, and faces two tests of loyalty after leaving power.

nodes.title: Duryodhana
nodes.summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī’s son. He challenges Pāṇḍava rule and refuses Kṛṣṇa’s settlement.

nodes.title: Bhīma
nodes.summary: A Pāṇḍava, brother of Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna. He challenges Yudhiṣṭhira in the hall and fights Duryodhana with a mace.

nodes.title: Arjuna
nodes.summary: A Pāṇḍava archer. Kṛṣṇa is his charioteer, Abhimanyu is his son, and Droṇa had taught him.

nodes.title: Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: A Yādava ally of the Pāṇḍavas. He moves from envoy to charioteer and counsellor. Gāndhārī later calls him to account.

nodes.title: Karṇa
nodes.summary: Kuntī’s firstborn, reared away from her. He stands with Duryodhana and eventually takes command. The brothers learn how he is related to them after he dies.

nodes.title: Vidura
nodes.summary: A Kuru adviser and the half-brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu. He warns the brothers about the house and opposes the use of the dice game.

nodes.title: Śakuni
nodes.summary: Gāndhārī’s brother and Duryodhana’s uncle. He plays the dice on Duryodhana’s side.

nodes.title: Vikarṇa
nodes.summary: A brother of Duryodhana. At the dice game he defies his own side’s ruling on Draupadī.

nodes.title: Droṇa
nodes.summary: Teacher of the rival Kuru cousins. He takes command of the Kaurava army after Bhīṣma falls.

nodes.title: Śikhaṇḍin
nodes.summary: A child of Drupada who fights for the Pāṇḍavas. Bhīṣma refuses to strike Śikhaṇḍin, giving Arjuna an opening.

nodes.title: Abhimanyu
nodes.summary: The son of Arjuna and Subhadrā. His death in the formation prompts Arjuna’s vow.

nodes.title: Jayadratha
nodes.summary: The Sindhu ruler and husband of Duryodhana’s sister Duḥśalā. He prevents Abhimanyu’s allies from following him.

nodes.title: Aśvatthāman
nodes.summary: Droṇa’s son. He survives the main battle and leads the attack on the camp.

nodes.title: Gāndhārī
nodes.summary: Mother of Duryodhana and wife of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. After mourning her sons she holds Kṛṣṇa to account and later leaves court.

nodes.title: Kuntī
nodes.summary: Mother of Karṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna. Before the battle she asks Karṇa to join his brothers. She leaves the restored court with the older Kuru couple.

nodes.title: Nala
nodes.summary: King of Niṣadha in Bṛhadaśva’s story. He loses his kingdom at dice and learns skills that let him recover it.

nodes.title: Damayantī
nodes.summary: A princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala. She devises a way to bring Nala back within reach after their separation.

nodes.title: Hastināpura
nodes.summary: Hastinapur, Uttar Pradesh. Modern archaeological site and traditional identification.

nodes.title: Vāraṇāvata
nodes.summary: Barnāwā area, Uttar Pradesh. Proposed literary identification.

nodes.title: Indraprastha
nodes.summary: Purana Qila, Delhi. Traditional identification discussed in excavation literature.

nodes.title: Pañcāla
nodes.summary: Broad western Uttar Pradesh reference point. Regional orientation only, site of the episode unlocated.

nodes.title: Kāmyaka
nodes.summary: Forest setting in the narrative. Map location left open.

nodes.title: Matsya
nodes.summary: Viratnagar area, Rajasthan. Traditional regional locator, exact court unverified.

nodes.title: Kurukṣetra
nodes.summary: Kurukshetra district, Haryana. Modern regional reference, battlefield extent unverified.

nodes.title: Dvārakā
nodes.summary: Dwarka, Gujarat. Modern coastal site; literary identification requires separate evidence.

nodes.title: Northern mountains
nodes.summary: Direction described in the story. Route and endpoint unlocated.

nodes.title: Who tells the Mahābhārata?
nodes.summary: A storyteller reports the tale he heard at a royal sacrifice.

nodes.title: The vow that changes the throne
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma renounces his claim and promises to remain unmarried so Śāntanu can marry Satyavatī. The promise changes who can inherit.

nodes.title: The house of lac
nodes.summary: The brothers face an engineered fire at Vāraṇāvata. Vidura’s warning helps them escape through a tunnel.

nodes.title: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara
nodes.summary: The Pāṇḍavas reach Pañcāla in disguise. Arjuna completes the trial at Draupadī’s svayaṃvara.

nodes.title: A new capital
nodes.summary: The Pāṇḍavas receive a share of the kingdom and establish Indraprastha. Their new court changes the rivalry between the families.

nodes.title: The dice match
nodes.summary: Śakuni plays on Duryodhana’s behalf. After Yudhiṣṭhira loses, Draupadī asks whether he had the authority to stake her.

nodes.title: Into the forest
nodes.summary: The brothers and Draupadī leave the court. The forest books follow their travels and the debates and stories told along the way.

nodes.title: A story within the exile
nodes.summary: Bṛhadaśva tells the exiled Yudhiṣṭhira about Nala and Damayantī. Their separation and reunion offer another way to understand the aftermath of a dice game.

nodes.title: The year in disguise
nodes.summary: The brothers and Draupadī live under assumed identities at Virāṭa’s court. A raid on the cattle puts their disguises at risk.

nodes.title: Kṛṣṇa’s peace mission
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa travels to the Kuru court to seek a settlement. The mission ends without an agreement and preparations for battle continue.

nodes.title: Karṇa answers Kuntī
nodes.summary: Kuntī tells Karṇa he is her son. He promises to spare four brothers but still chooses to fight Arjuna.

nodes.title: Vyāsa reads the omens
nodes.summary: Vyāsa describes disturbing signs to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. One verse mentions Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha, and nearby passages mention planets and the luminaries.

nodes.title: Arjuna stops the chariot
nodes.summary: Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to stop between the armies. Seeing family, teachers, and friends on both sides, he questions whether to fight.

nodes.title: Bhīṣma falls
nodes.summary: Arjuna advances with Śikhaṇḍin. Bhīṣma is brought down and remains on a bed of arrows.

nodes.title: Droṇa takes command
nodes.summary: Duryodhana asks Karṇa who can lead the army after Bhīṣma falls. Karṇa proposes Droṇa.

nodes.title: Abhimanyu enters the formation
nodes.summary: Abhimanyu enters Droṇa’s formation. He is separated from help and killed, leading to Arjuna’s vow.

nodes.title: The vow and the darkening sky
nodes.summary: Arjuna must reach Jayadratha before sunset. Ganguli’s rendering describes darkness produced through yoga, a scene sometimes read as an eclipse.

nodes.title: Droṇa lays down his weapons
nodes.summary: The report of Aśvatthāman’s death breaks Droṇa’s resolve. Dhṛṣṭadyumna attacks after he casts down his weapons.

nodes.title: Karṇa leads the surviving army
nodes.summary: After Droṇa’s death, Karṇa lines up Duryodhana’s army at dawn.

nodes.title: Arjuna and Karṇa
nodes.summary: Karṇa’s chariot wheel sinks during the duel. The scene turns on a dispute over the rules of battle.

nodes.title: The final duel
nodes.summary: Bhīma and Duryodhana fight with maces. The closing blow prompts arguments about how the duel was won.

nodes.title: The sleeping camp
nodes.summary: Aśvatthāman enters the enemy camp at night. The attack targets survivors of the battle.

nodes.title: Gāndhārī on the battlefield
nodes.summary: Gāndhārī and the other bereaved women walk among the fallen. This is the aftermath as seen by families.

nodes.title: The brother they did not know
nodes.summary: At the water rites, Kuntī asks the Pāṇḍavas to mourn Karṇa as their eldest brother.

nodes.title: Lessons in kingship
nodes.summary: While Bhīṣma lies wounded, Yudhiṣṭhira seeks guidance on ruling and on the duties that come with power.

nodes.title: When a ruler is in danger
nodes.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira asks what a weak king can do when allies and resources have gone.

nodes.title: What can wait until tomorrow?
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma tells of a son who challenges his father’s assumption that he can postpone the search for liberation.

nodes.title: What makes a gift matter?
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma praises giving land and retells Nārada’s argument for the importance of giving food.

nodes.title: Bhīṣma’s death
nodes.summary: After teaching Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma chooses the time of his death. The interval and seasonal wording enter Oak’s dating argument.

nodes.title: The horse sacrifice
nodes.summary: The horse’s journey links the restored court to other rulers. Arjuna travels with it and faces challenges along the way.

nodes.title: The elders withdraw
nodes.summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, and Kuntī leave the court for forest life. Yudhiṣṭhira later learns how they died.

nodes.title: The end of Dvārakā
nodes.summary: The book follows the destruction of the Yādavas and the loss of Dvārakā. Literary accounts and the dating of marine finds are distinct questions.

nodes.title: The last journey
nodes.summary: The Pāṇḍavas leave the throne and go north. Yudhiṣṭhira refuses to abandon the dog that follows him.

nodes.title: The final test
nodes.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira is confronted with an unexpected picture of heaven and hell. The book closes by revealing the purpose of that test.

nodes.title: War day 2
nodes.summary: After the first day’s withdrawal, Yudhiṣṭhira fears defeat. The Pāṇḍavas deploy a crane-shaped formation. Duryodhana responds by drawing his commanders together against it.

nodes.title: War day 3
nodes.summary: As the Pāṇḍava lines scatter, Kṛṣṇa leaves his chariot with his discus and rushes at Bhīṣma. Arjuna catches and restrains him, then renews his own attack.

nodes.title: War day 4
nodes.summary: Bhīma breaks the elephant force. Duryodhana orders the other troops to concentrate on him, turning an elephant attack into a wider assault.

nodes.title: War day 5
nodes.summary: Śikhaṇḍin and Virāṭa confront Bhīṣma. The encounter brings Śikhaṇḍin against the commander before the two sides use that pairing decisively on day 10.

nodes.title: War day 6
nodes.summary: Duryodhana’s brothers surround Bhīma, whom Sañjaya compares to the sun surrounded by planets. The fighting follows Sañjaya’s warning to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that the war follows from the dice game.

nodes.title: War day 7
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma forms the Kaurava array at sunrise. As Arjuna disrupts their side’s ranks, Duryodhana rallies the Kaurava warriors and Bhīṣma moves to oppose him.

nodes.title: War day 8
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma leads a formation compared to an ocean, with Droṇa and Bhagadatta behind him. After heavy losses Duryodhana consults his allies that evening about defeating the Pāṇḍavas.

nodes.title: War day 9
nodes.summary: The army reassembles after Duryodhana and Bhīṣma’s difficult conversation. After the day’s damage the Pāṇḍavas seek Bhīṣma’s advice, and he tells them how to bring him down.

nodes.title: War day 12
nodes.summary: Arjuna hears Bhagadatta’s elephants breaking the ranks and turns toward the main battle. Bhagadatta falls in their encounter, while Droṇa’s effort to capture Yudhiṣṭhira goes on.

nodes.title: 3.32 · Yudhiṣṭhira replies to Draupadī
nodes.summary: Draupadī has asked why good conduct has brought them so much pain. Yudhiṣṭhira says he gives because giving is called for. For him, the chance of gaining a reward is irrelevant to the choice.

nodes.title: 5.72 · Bhīma asks Kṛṣṇa to speak gently
nodes.summary: Bhīma asks the envoy to seek peace and avoid threatening war. He expects Duryodhana to be slow to change his mind, so he urges Kṛṣṇa to try persuasion.

nodes.title: 7.17 · The oath-bound fighters draw Arjuna away
nodes.summary: The oath-bound fighters arrange their chariots in a half-moon and cheer as Arjuna comes toward them. Arjuna recognizes the Trigartas and advances on their line.

nodes.title: 11.16 · Gāndhārī surveys the battlefield
nodes.summary: The narrative gives Gāndhārī a sight that brings the distant battlefield close. Sañjaya’s account of combat gives way to a mother looking at the bodies left behind.

nodes.title: 12.57 · When can a ruler oppose an ally?
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma weighs whom a ruler should reconcile with and whom to oppose. He argues that a friend or teacher who harms the kingdom can be resisted and cites King Sagara’s treatment of his own son.

nodes.title: 1.1 · Who first tells this story?
nodes.summary: Ugraśravas arrives after hearing Vaiśampāyana recite Vyāsa’s narrative at Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice. The first audience asks where he has come from.

nodes.title: 1.94 · Devavrata’s two promises
nodes.summary: Devavrata yields the succession to any child of Satyavatī. The fisherman worries about a later claim by Devavrata’s own children, so Devavrata also pledges lifelong celibacy.

nodes.title: 1.199 · A second Kuru capital
nodes.summary: The king tells the brothers to avoid another dispute by occupying Khāṇḍavaprastha. Having received half the realm, the returning brothers establish the city named Indraprastha.

nodes.title: 2.54 · The first losses
nodes.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira begins this series with gold, then wagers vehicles, elephants, people in household service and other royal resources. Each declared loss leads to another stake.

nodes.title: 2.58 · When the stake becomes a person
nodes.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira stakes his brothers in order, then himself. Śakuni tells the already defeated king to stake Draupadī to recover himself and finally declares that wager won.

nodes.title: 2.60 · Who had authority to stake Draupadī?
nodes.summary: Draupadī asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before he staked her. Bhīṣma names conflicting assumptions about property and a husband’s authority, then says he cannot decide the question.

nodes.title: 2.61 · Vikarṇa and Karṇa dispute the wager
nodes.summary: Vikarṇa argues that Draupadī remains unwon, citing the order of losses, pressure on the gambler and her marriage to all five brothers. Karṇa interprets the elders’ silence as assent and attacks Vikarṇa’s argument.

nodes.title: 2.66 · The wager of years
nodes.summary: With the brothers released, Duryodhana argues that they will retaliate and proposes another game. Its terms are twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year without recognition.

nodes.title: 3.27 · A gathering in Dvaita forest
nodes.summary: Brahmins gather around the Pāṇḍavas, and the account sets the sound of their recitation beside that of bowstrings. Baka Dālbhya addresses the king among the seers.

nodes.title: 3.28 · Draupadī asks about anger
nodes.summary: Draupadī recalls how Duryodhana watched the family depart. She contrasts the king’s conduct with what it has earned and challenges him over his restraint.

nodes.title: 3.31 · Does good conduct guarantee a good outcome?
nodes.summary: Draupadī knows duty matters more to Yudhiṣṭhira than kingdom or family. His undeserved suffering makes her question how wealth and distress are actually distributed.

nodes.title: 3.50 · Why tell Yudhiṣṭhira about Nala?
nodes.summary: The sage introduces Nala, king of Niṣadha, and Damayantī, a princess of Vidarbha. Their virtues and the report each hears about the other prepare their meeting.

nodes.title: 3.281 · Sāvitrī follows Yama
nodes.summary: Satyavān grows weak as he chops wood. Sāvitrī supports him as he sinks down; the encounter with Yama turns her vigil into an extended negotiation.

nodes.title: 3.296 · The price of drinking first
nodes.summary: The brothers need water. A voice warns them to answer questions before drinking, but thirst and attempts to use force override the warning. Each who drinks falls.

nodes.title: 3.297 · A ruler answers the yakṣa
nodes.summary: Seeing no marks of weapons, Yudhiṣṭhira seeks a cause. He accepts questions before drinking and ultimately chooses Nakula when offered one brother, reasoning that each of his father’s wives should still have a son.

nodes.title: 4.1 · Choosing names for the incognito year
nodes.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira chooses to become Kaṅka, a man known to play dice. The strategy uses each person’s skills while disguising rank and kinship.

nodes.title: 5.7 · Choosing between Kṛṣṇa and his force
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa offers soldiers to one side and his own unarmed presence to the other. Arjuna chooses Kṛṣṇa. Duryodhana leaves with the force, and Balarāma declines to fight for either cousin.

nodes.title: 5.33 · Why can the king not sleep?
nodes.summary: The king asks to hear what is right. Vidura starts by asking whether anxiety over another person’s wealth is robbing him of sleep, then turns to how wise and reckless people act.

nodes.title: 5.70 · The proposal for five villages
nodes.summary: Yudhiṣṭhira lays out a small territorial demand so the two groups can survive without fighting. He names four places and leaves the fifth open.

nodes.title: 5.125 · Duryodhana rejects the settlement
nodes.summary: Duryodhana refuses to concede land, even the ground that a needle point would pierce. The statement makes clear how little room the envoy has to negotiate.

nodes.title: 5.144 · Why Karṇa stays
nodes.summary: He says changing sides now would look like fear and would abandon those depending on him. He still promises Kuntī to spare four of her sons if he can.

nodes.title: 6.2 · Vyāsa speaks to Dhṛtarāṣṭra
nodes.summary: The chapter gathers troubling descriptions including the Moon and a reversal in the relation of Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha. The signs sit together in a speech before the battle report.

nodes.title: 6.23 · Arjuna looks at both armies
nodes.summary: Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to stop the chariot and see who is gathered. The ranks contain those he owes duties to as relatives, pupils and teachers.

nodes.title: 7.35 · The opening in the formation
nodes.summary: Abhimanyu breaks through in front of Droṇa. The text then describes warriors and troops surrounding him after he enters.

nodes.title: 7.165 · The teacher puts down his bow
nodes.summary: The account moves from the misleading report about Droṇa’s son to his decision to cast off his weapons after Bhīma speaks. Dhṛṣṭadyumna takes the opening.

nodes.title: 8.67 · Who may invoke the rules of battle?
nodes.summary: Karṇa’s wheel has sunk. Kṛṣṇa answers his appeal to dharma by recalling Draupadī in the assembly and the party that used the dice game.

nodes.title: 9.57 · The blow in the mace duel
nodes.summary: The narrative recalls Bhīma’s vow to break Duryodhana’s thighs and depicts him doing so. The blow brings the contest to a close.

nodes.title: 10.8 · The attack on the sleeping camp
nodes.summary: Aśvatthāman enters at night. His companions guard the exits while he attacks a camp whose warriors believe the day’s battle has ended.

nodes.title: 11.27 · Kuntī asks the brothers to mourn Karṇa
nodes.summary: She tells the Pāṇḍavas that the man they fought as Karṇa was their elder brother. Yudhiṣṭhira asks why they learned this only after his death.

nodes.title: 12.56 · Effort, fortune, and trust
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma says effort and fate both matter but asks Yudhiṣṭhira to focus on what a ruler can do. He identifies truth as a source of trust.

nodes.title: 12.128 · How does duty change in a crisis?
nodes.summary: The depleted king is pressed by a stronger opponent. Bhīṣma considers how the treasury and force depend on each other and when relief should follow emergency demands.

nodes.title: 12.129 · When should a king give up the capital?
nodes.summary: He distinguishes an opponent who can be negotiated with from one whose aims make agreement harder. He weighs agreeing to terms and leaving the capital to survive.

nodes.title: 12.169 · Can liberation wait?
nodes.summary: The father describes a sequence of life duties. The son argues that ageing and death can interrupt any plan that leaves the search for what is good until later.

nodes.title: 12.253 · Why does an ascetic visit a merchant?
nodes.summary: Jājali’s ascetic self-confidence is checked when he hears that Tulādhāra is his superior in dharma. He goes to Vārāṇasī and finds the merchant selling ordinary goods.

nodes.title: 13.61 · A gift that keeps yielding
nodes.summary: Bhīṣma praises land for what it can keep producing. His examples include crops, livestock and materials that sustain a livelihood.

nodes.title: 13.62 · A gift that meets a need immediately
nodes.summary: Nārada argues that food supports householders and mendicants alike. The gift helps because their continued life depends on it.

nodes.title: 13.153 · The teacher waits for a turning point
nodes.summary: The chapter refers to the Sun turning north. Bhīṣma counts the nights spent lying on the arrows and names Māgha.

nodes.title: 14.78 · Arjuna meets the son who must oppose him
nodes.summary: Babhruvāhana greets his father Arjuna. The ritual surrounding the wandering horse gives Arjuna reason to demand a challenge, and Ulūpī urges the younger man to fight.

nodes.title: 15.45 · Nārada brings news from the forest
nodes.summary: A wind feeds a forest fire. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and Kuntī remain, while Sañjaya escapes.

nodes.title: 16.8 · Leaving Dvārakā
nodes.summary: Arjuna warns the inhabitants that the sea will cover Dvārakā and helps organize their departure. The narrative then describes the city filling with water.

nodes.title: 17.3 · A place in heaven with a condition
nodes.summary: Indra offers passage to heaven if the dog is left behind. Yudhiṣṭhira refuses to abandon a being that has depended on him.

nodes.title: 18.3 · Indra explains the final test
nodes.summary: Indra explains the king’s experience by recalling the misleading report about Droṇa’s son. Dharma acknowledges the conduct Yudhiṣṭhira showed during the ordeal.

nodes.title: Mandodarī
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa’s wife. Her lament shows the war’s effect on the defeated household.

nodes.title: Kuśa
nodes.summary: One of Sītā’s twin sons. Vālmīki names him in the forest.

nodes.title: Lava
nodes.summary: One of Sītā’s twin sons. He is raised with Kuśa at the hermitage.

nodes.title: Sītā
nodes.summary: Janaka’s daughter. She chooses exile, questions Hanumān about the rescue, and speaks for herself at the final gathering.

nodes.title: Rāma
nodes.summary: Daśaratha’s son. His response to the promises of the court drives the exile and later tests of kingship.

nodes.title: Lakṣmaṇa
nodes.summary: Rāma’s brother and companion in the forest. He carries out the second exile order in Uttara.

nodes.title: Bharata
nodes.summary: Kaikeyī’s son. He seeks Rāma’s return and takes the sandals as a sign of the elder brother’s authority.

nodes.title: Hanumān
nodes.summary: Sugrīva’s messenger and the envoy who finds Sītā in Laṅkā.

nodes.title: Sugrīva
nodes.summary: Vāli’s brother. His alliance with Rāma helps him recover Kiṣkindhā.

nodes.title: Vāli
nodes.summary: The ruler who challenges Rāma’s reasons for intervening in his fight with Sugrīva.

nodes.title: Kaikeyī
nodes.summary: Daśaratha’s wife and Bharata’s mother. She invokes the promises he made to her.

nodes.title: Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: Ruler of Laṅkā and Vibhīṣaṇa’s brother. He abducts Sītā from the forest.

nodes.title: Vibhīṣaṇa
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa’s brother. He seeks refuge with Rāma and joins the coalition.

nodes.title: Janaka
nodes.summary: King of Mithilā and Sītā’s father. He tells of finding her during the ploughing.

nodes.title: Vālmīki
nodes.summary: The poet who opens the work with a question. His hermitage provides a new setting in Uttara.

nodes.title: Jaṭāyu
nodes.summary: An ally of the exiles who confronts Rāvaṇa during Sītā’s abduction.

nodes.title: Nala the builder
nodes.summary: The figure commissioned to build the sea crossing in Yuddhakāṇḍa.

nodes.title: Śatrughna
nodes.summary: Daśaratha’s son accompanies Bharata and later asks Cyavana about Lavaṇa’s power.

nodes.title: Ayodhyā
nodes.summary: Modern city reference. The modern city gives an orientation point for the literary capital in Kosala.

nodes.title: Mithilā
nodes.summary: Traditional regional reference. Janakpur is used as a reference for the Mithilā tradition. The geography of a narrated royal household is unresolved.

nodes.title: Gaṅgā crossing
nodes.summary: Textual route stage. The river is named in the narrative. The atlas leaves the exact crossing point open.

nodes.title: Citrakūṭa
nodes.summary: Traditional pilgrimage area. The marker is an approximate modern regional reference for Chitrakoot rather than a hermitage location.

nodes.title: Pañcavaṭī
nodes.summary: Traditional association. Panchavati in present-day Nashik is a pilgrimage association. The story’s house and abduction site are not independently located.

nodes.title: Kiṣkindhā
nodes.summary: Traditional regional association. The Hampi area is an orientation point for the Kiṣkindhā tradition. UNESCO documents the later historic monuments at Hampi.

nodes.title: Laṅkā and the Aśoka grove
nodes.summary: Literary location. The route follows the names in the text. The location of the palace and grove remains open.

nodes.title: Palk Strait shoals
nodes.summary: Modern study region. The point represents the ridge between Dhanushkodi and Talaimannar. The remote-sensing study measured present-day bathymetry.

nodes.title: Vālmīki’s question
nodes.summary: The poem opens with a question about virtue, courage and truthful conduct. Nārada answers by naming Rāma and gives a short account of the story before it unfolds at length.

nodes.title: 1.1 · Vālmīki’s question
nodes.summary: Vālmīki asks Nārada about a person whose conduct is worth knowing.

nodes.title: The gods prepare allies for Rāma
nodes.summary: After Viṣṇu undertakes to become the king’s son, the gods are asked to create helpers. The speech describes the strength, judgement, and capacity to change form that the future allies will need.

nodes.title: 1.16 · The gods prepare allies for Rāma
nodes.summary: The Self-born deity addresses the assembled gods.

nodes.title: The birth of the princes
nodes.summary: Kauśalyā bears Rāma. The Baroda main text gives a brief birth description at this point. The Southern Recension preserves a longer birth passage with Caitra Navamī and a reference to Aditi’s asterism.

nodes.title: 1.17 · The birth of the princes
nodes.summary: The narrator introduces the sons of Daśaratha.

nodes.title: Janaka tells where Sītā came from
nodes.summary: As Janaka ploughs the ground he finds a girl. His account connects her name with the furrow and sets up the conditions he lays down for her marriage.

nodes.title: 1.65 · Janaka tells where Sītā came from
nodes.summary: Janaka recounts what happened while preparing a field.

nodes.title: Janaka joins the households
nodes.summary: Janaka offers Sītā to Rāma and directs the joining of hands. The marriage passage also joins the other princes and brides of the two households.

nodes.title: 1.72 · Janaka joins the households
nodes.summary: Janaka addresses the princes at the marriage.

nodes.title: The coronation becomes exile
nodes.summary: Kaikeyī uses two saved boons to seek Bharata’s installation and Rāma’s departure to the forest for fourteen years. Rāma agrees to go in order to keep Daśaratha’s word.

nodes.title: 2.16 · The coronation becomes exile
nodes.summary: Kaikeyī explains the old promise to Rāma.

nodes.title: Sītā chooses to go
nodes.summary: Rāma has explained why she should remain in the city. Sītā answers that the circumstances of a wife are bound to those of her husband and treats his exile as hers too.

nodes.title: 2.24 · Sītā chooses to go
nodes.summary: Sītā replies to Rāma in Ayodhyā.

nodes.title: Rāma lists the risks of the forest
nodes.summary: He tells her that the forest brings hardship and makes a case for her staying behind. His appeal puts everyday conditions, not simply court protocol, into the discussion.

nodes.title: 2.25 · Rāma lists the risks of the forest
nodes.summary: Rāma asks Sītā to reconsider.

nodes.title: Crossing the Gaṅgā
nodes.summary: The three cross the river during the departure from Kosala. Sītā addresses the river on the crossing. The chapter records a journey stage, with routes still uncertain in modern geography.

nodes.title: 2.46 · Crossing the Gaṅgā
nodes.summary: Rāma speaks to Lakṣmaṇa as the party reaches the water.

nodes.title: Bharata takes the sandals
nodes.summary: Bharata asks Rāma to step into the sandals, then receives them. The reunion does not persuade Rāma to end his father’s promised term of exile.

nodes.title: 2.104 · Bharata takes the sandals
nodes.summary: Bharata requests a token from Rāma.

nodes.title: Bharata leaves with the sandals
nodes.summary: Bharata lifts the sandals onto his head, then mounts his chariot with Śatrughna. His party follows the Mandākinī and calls at Bharadvāja’s hermitage on the return journey.

nodes.title: 2.105 · Bharata leaves with the sandals
nodes.summary: The narrator follows Bharata’s party as it leaves Citrakūṭa.

nodes.title: Making a home in Pañcavaṭī
nodes.summary: Rāma identifies the wooded place and asks Lakṣmaṇa to select ground for a dwelling. The account describes a living place in the forest, before it becomes the scene of separation.

nodes.title: 3.14 · Making a home in Pañcavaṭī
nodes.summary: Rāma addresses Lakṣmaṇa as the three arrive.

nodes.title: Lakṣmaṇa describes the cold season
nodes.summary: Autumn has ended. On the way to the river, Lakṣmaṇa describes mist, ripening crops, cold water and the welcome warmth of a fire.

nodes.title: 3.15 · Lakṣmaṇa describes the cold season
nodes.summary: Lakṣmaṇa speaks on the way to the Godāvarī with Rāma and Sītā.

nodes.title: Rāvaṇa reveals his disguise
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa abandons the guise of an ascetic, seizes Sītā and places her in his vehicle. She calls to those who might hear and names the place she is being taken from.

nodes.title: 3.47 · Rāvaṇa reveals his disguise
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa speaks to Sītā, who calls out as he takes her.

nodes.title: Jaṭāyu confronts Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: The great bird wakes, names himself and challenges the attempt to take Sītā. His intervention turns the abduction into a fight that the searchers will learn about afterward.

nodes.title: 3.48 · Jaṭāyu confronts Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: Jaṭāyu answers Sītā’s cry and addresses Rāvaṇa.

nodes.title: Hanumān speaks to the strangers
nodes.summary: Hanumān is sent to find out who has arrived. He introduces himself after speaking with the two exiles. Their meeting creates a way to negotiate with Sugrīva.

nodes.title: 4.3 · Hanumān speaks to the strangers
nodes.summary: Hanumān approaches Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa for Sugrīva.

nodes.title: Rāma and Sugrīva make an alliance
nodes.summary: Sugrīva extends his hand. The two walk around the fire to seal their bond. Each needs help that the other can offer.

nodes.title: 4.5 · Rāma and Sugrīva make an alliance
nodes.summary: Sugrīva offers friendship. Hanumān prepares a fire.

nodes.title: Vāli asks who can punish him
nodes.summary: Vāli asks why Rāma struck him when he was fighting somebody else. He questions the ruler’s jurisdiction and whether outward signs of virtue match this act.

nodes.title: 4.17 · Vāli asks who can punish him
nodes.summary: The wounded Vāli challenges Rāma about the shot.

nodes.title: Rāma answers Vāli
nodes.summary: He invokes the ruler’s power to punish wrongdoing and characterizes Vāli’s conduct toward his brother’s household as a violation. His argument depends on authority that Vāli had questioned.

nodes.title: 4.18 · Rāma answers Vāli
nodes.summary: Rāma replies to Vāli’s accusations.

nodes.title: Hanumān reminds Sugrīva of the agreement
nodes.summary: Sugrīva worries that keeping friends is harder than making them. Hanumān reminds him what Rāma did for the alliance and says the season for action has arrived.

nodes.title: 4.31 · Hanumān reminds Sugrīva of the agreement
nodes.summary: Sugrīva and Hanumān speak before the ministers.

nodes.title: Hanumān takes the sea crossing
nodes.summary: Hanumān prepares to cross the sea to look for Sītā. The search that had stopped at the shore becomes a single messenger’s journey.

nodes.title: 5.1 · Hanumān takes the sea crossing
nodes.summary: The narrator follows Hanumān as he begins the task.

nodes.title: Hanumān enters the Aśoka grove
nodes.summary: He examines the grove and the surroundings in which he hopes to find the captive. The description gives the reader a setting for the later meeting.

nodes.title: 5.12 · Hanumān enters the Aśoka grove
nodes.summary: Hanumān searches the landscape inside Laṅkā.

nodes.title: Sītā recognizes the ring
nodes.summary: Hanumān shows Rāma’s inscribed ring. Sītā questions him about Rāma’s safety and whether he is taking steps to gain help.

nodes.title: 5.34 · Sītā recognizes the ring
nodes.summary: Hanumān offers the ring. Sītā asks about allies and preparations.

nodes.title: Sītā tells Hanumān how much time is left
nodes.summary: Sītā is glad Rāma remembers her and grieved that he suffers. She says two months remain before Rāvaṇa’s deadline and asks Hanumān to tell Rāma to hurry. She reports that Vibhīṣaṇa has urged her return.

nodes.title: 5.35 · Sītā tells Hanumān how much time is left
nodes.summary: Sītā speaks to Hanumān after accepting the ring.

nodes.title: The sky described during the march
nodes.summary: The passage names Brahmarāśi among other sky markers. Oak identifies it with Vega. The identity and a tolerable angular distance from the pole are questions a model must state explicitly.

nodes.title: 6.4 · The sky described during the march
nodes.summary: The campaign narrative includes a description of the sky.

nodes.title: Rāma decides whether to grant shelter
nodes.summary: Vibhīṣaṇa’s break with his brother Rāvaṇa makes the allies consider whether they can trust him. Rāma states a rule of accepting someone who comes seeking protection.

nodes.title: 6.12 · Rāma decides whether to grant shelter
nodes.summary: Rāma tells the allies how he will treat an appeal for refuge.

nodes.title: Nala leads the crossing work
nodes.summary: Nala organizes the work and the force reaches the far shore. The story uses a comparison with a line through the sea to describe the completed crossing.

nodes.title: 6.15 · Nala leads the crossing work
nodes.summary: The ocean proposes Nala as builder. The narration describes the bridge.

nodes.title: Rāma and Rāvaṇa remain in the field
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa keeps changing weapons when one fails. The account compares the shining discs in the air to the Sun, Moon and other celestial bodies. Rāma breaks them as the duel continues.

nodes.title: 6.88 · Rāma and Rāvaṇa remain in the field
nodes.summary: The narrator follows the exchanges between the two opponents.

nodes.title: Mandodarī mourns Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: She recalls the ruler’s extraordinary power and asks how a man who lived in the forest could bring him down. Her words give the defeated household a voice after the battle.

nodes.title: 6.99 · Mandodarī mourns Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: Mandodarī speaks after seeing Rāvaṇa killed.

nodes.title: Sītā answers after the battle
nodes.summary: With Rāvaṇa defeated, the reunion becomes a public questioning of Sītā. She calls on the fire as witness to her conduct and enters it. The people watching witness her choice.

nodes.title: 6.104 · Sītā answers after the battle
nodes.summary: Sītā speaks and enters the fire after Rāma’s public challenge.

nodes.title: The return looks back across the sea
nodes.summary: The homeward passage names the bridge and points out places connected with the campaign. It recounts stages from the route after the fighting has ended.

nodes.title: 6.111 · The return looks back across the sea
nodes.summary: Rāma speaks to Sītā on the way back.

nodes.title: Bharata returns authority
nodes.summary: Bharata gives the kingdom back. He compares the task of carrying it alone to a young animal struggling with the heavy load of a stronger one.

nodes.title: 6.116 · Bharata returns authority
nodes.summary: Bharata addresses Rāma after his return.

nodes.title: Rāma orders a second exile
nodes.summary: He fears continuing public reproach and orders Lakṣmaṇa to take Sītā beyond the realm and leave her near Vālmīki’s hermitage. Sītā is given no voice in the order.

nodes.title: 7.44 · Rāma orders a second exile
nodes.summary: Rāma instructs Lakṣmaṇa after hearing reports from the city.

nodes.title: Vālmīki names Sītā’s twins
nodes.summary: The sage uses kuśa grass and blade cuttings in a protective rite and names the twins Kuśa and Lava. The account explains the names through the items used in the rite.

nodes.title: 7.58 · Vālmīki names Sītā’s twins
nodes.summary: The young people of the hermitage tell Vālmīki that Sītā has given birth.

nodes.title: Cyavana tells Śatrughna about Lavaṇa
nodes.summary: Śatrughna wants to know how powerful Lavaṇa’s weapon is. Cyavana tells him about the king Māndhātā, whose claim to universal rule met its limit in Madhu’s forest.

nodes.title: 7.59 · Cyavana tells Śatrughna about Lavaṇa
nodes.summary: Śatrughna asks a question. Cyavana answers with the story of Māndhātā.

nodes.title: Sītā calls on the earth
nodes.summary: Sītā declares her fidelity and asks the earth to receive her. The narration then describes a throne rising from the ground.

nodes.title: 7.88 · Sītā calls on the earth
nodes.summary: Sītā speaks for herself before the gathered company.

nodes.title: Oak’s identification of Brahmarāśi
nodes.summary: Oak identifies this marker as Abhijit and tests Vega’s distance from the pole.

nodes.title: The Deccan before Swarajya
nodes.summary: The Adil Shahi and Nizam Shahi courts and the Mughal advance shaped opportunities for landed families, military service and negotiations.

nodes.title: The formation of Swarajya
nodes.summary: Fort acquisition, diplomacy and the assertion of royal authority gave Shivaji Maharaj a base against competing powers.

nodes.title: Succession and resistance
nodes.summary: Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai faced an expanding Mughal military presence. Leadership moved when a capital or fort could no longer serve.

nodes.title: Rival courts and revenue rights
nodes.summary: Shahu’s release opened a fight over succession. His court made agreements about tribute and revenue while the Kolhapur line retained authority.

nodes.title: Expansion and administration
nodes.summary: Maratha chiefs and revenue agents operated across different regions. Peshwa authority interacted with local elites and other ruling houses.

nodes.title: The north, Panipat and the return
nodes.summary: The campaign depended on other rulers, supply, money and movement. Defeat interrupted the northern push, which was later renewed.

nodes.title: Regional powers and Company rivalry
nodes.summary: Shinde, Holkar, Gaikwad and Bhonsle interests diverged. The Peshwa and the East India Company became entangled in competing agreements.

nodes.title: Company treaties and war
nodes.summary: Successive agreements increased Company leverage. War in 1817–18 ended the Peshwa’s political authority.

nodes.title: Authority continues in other forms
nodes.summary: Satara retained a ruling house under Company paramountcy until annexation. The end of the Peshwa’s government did not end Maratha political and social institutions.

nodes.title: Deccan sultanate country
nodes.summary: Regional context. No fixed frontier drawn. Offices, forts and estates had different holders at different dates.

nodes.title: Pratapgad
nodes.summary: Modern fort reference. A hill-forest fort in the UNESCO property. The marker orients the reader to the site.

nodes.title: Agra
nodes.summary: Modern city reference. The point does not identify the building in which Shivaji was detained.

nodes.title: Rajgad
nodes.summary: Modern fort reference. A separate hill-fort component near Raigad. The point shows geography and terrain context.

nodes.title: Suvarnadurg
nodes.summary: Modern maritime fort reference. A fortified coastal position in the same modern heritage collection.

nodes.title: Gingee
nodes.summary: Modern fort reference. The Tamil Nadu component of the inscribed property. Used here to orient the reader to Rajaram’s southern base.

nodes.title: Satara
nodes.summary: Modern city reference. Orientation point for Shahu’s court and the later princely state.

nodes.title: Vasai (Bassein)
nodes.summary: Modern fort and port reference. The names Vasai and Bassein refer to the same place in different records. It has distinct episodes of military seizure, revenue and diplomacy.

nodes.title: Pune
nodes.summary: Modern city reference. Orientation point for the Peshwa’s government and the 1817 treaty.

nodes.title: Delhi
nodes.summary: Modern city reference. The point orients the northern campaign and the 1719 documentary context. It does not trace the route of the armies.

nodes.title: Panipat
nodes.summary: Modern city reference. The city is a reference for the campaign and battle. Camp extent and precise movements are unresolved in this map.

nodes.title: Kunjpura
nodes.summary: Approximate modern locality. The district gazetteer names the locality in the October 1760 campaign. No battle footprint is drawn.

nodes.title: Khed in the succession account
nodes.summary: Named historical locality. The gazetteer names Khed. No exact battlefield position is assigned here.

nodes.title: Service and power in the Deccan
nodes.summary: The royal houses of Bijapur and Ahmadnagar, Mughal officers and local military families negotiated overlapping rights and service. Shahaji’s career belongs to this context.

nodes.title: Confrontation at Pratapgad
nodes.summary: Bijapur sent Afzal Khan against Shivaji. Their confrontation at Pratapgad became a turning point in the contest over forts and authority.

nodes.title: Agra and the escape
nodes.summary: Letters from Jaipur’s representatives record Shivaji’s escape. Accounts give different amounts of detail on how it occurred.

nodes.title: Sambhaji and Mughal pressure
nodes.summary: Sambhaji succeeded Shivaji and faced Aurangzeb’s southward campaigns. His capture and execution in 1689 brought another crisis for the court.

nodes.title: Rajaram’s southern base
nodes.summary: Rajaram reached the fortified base at Gingee under Mughal pressure in the Deccan. The southern stronghold let leadership continue while operations elsewhere remained contested.

nodes.title: Tarabai organizes resistance
nodes.summary: After Rajaram’s death, Tarabai acted for her young son and maintained a competing claim to rule during the struggle with the Mughals.

nodes.title: Allegiance changes at Khed
nodes.summary: As Shahu advanced, Dhanaji Jadhav did not engage his force, according to the district gazetteer. Parashurampant Pratinidhi withdrew toward Satara.

nodes.title: Shahu returns and claims the throne
nodes.summary: Released after Aurangzeb’s death, Sambhaji’s son Shahu claimed the throne. Some commanders supported him, while Tarabai held to the claim of her own son.

nodes.title: A right to collect revenue
nodes.summary: Grants secured through Balaji Vishwanath’s mission recognized claims to chauth and sardeshmukhi from six Deccan provinces. These were revenue claims that had to be collected in practice.

nodes.title: Vasai changes hands
nodes.summary: After a siege led by Chimaji Appa, the Portuguese lost Vasai. The change concerned a fort and a port with commercial and administrative needs.

nodes.title: A port ledger records trade and diplomacy
nodes.summary: The account records money and goods credited after the seizure of English ships in the previous year. It then records an instruction to return the goods because relations were friendly.

nodes.title: Shahu chooses Balaji Baji Rao
nodes.summary: After Baji Rao died, Shahu appointed his son Balaji Baji Rao. The Peshwa’s office became increasingly influential as operations extended into northern and eastern regions.

nodes.title: The move from Delhi to Kunjpura
nodes.summary: Bhāu’s force moved from Delhi towards Kunjpura. Blocking sources of money and provisions was a concern for both sides along the Yamunā.

nodes.title: The camp loses supply access
nodes.summary: Interdiction made food and fodder harder to bring into the Maratha camp. The burden extended to non-combatant followers and to animals needed for transport.

nodes.title: The Third Battle of Panipat
nodes.summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani’s coalition defeated the Maratha expedition. The Rohilla leaders and Shujāʿ al-Dawla had their own political interests in joining the coalition.

nodes.title: A renewed northern campaign
nodes.summary: Later Maratha intervention in the north restored influence around Delhi. It depended on leadership, funding and new negotiations.

nodes.title: Regional houses take different paths
nodes.summary: Military leaders and family houses built power bases with different ties to the Peshwa’s court. They negotiated with local rulers and increasingly with the Company.

nodes.title: Treaty of Bassein
nodes.summary: Baji Rao II sought Company support after defeat near Pune. The treaty provided for a subsidiary force and limited independent dealings with European rivals.

nodes.title: The Poona Treaty narrows the Peshwa’s options
nodes.summary: The archive lists a contemporary comparison of the Poona Treaty with Bassein. The agreement came before renewed fighting in 1817–18.

nodes.title: The Peshwa’s government ends
nodes.summary: The Company defeated and displaced Baji Rao II. The change ended the Peshwa’s government and rearranged relations with other authorities.

nodes.title: Satara under Company paramountcy
nodes.summary: Satara’s ruling house held a princely state under Company paramountcy after the Peshwa’s government ended. Annexation followed in 1848.

nodes.title: Shivaji Maharaj
nodes.summary: Founded Swarajya and made Raigad his capital.

nodes.title: Sambhaji
nodes.summary: Succeeded Shivaji while Mughal pressure intensified.

nodes.title: Rajaram
nodes.summary: Took leadership to a fortified base in the south.

nodes.title: Tarabai
nodes.summary: Led resistance and acted for her son after Rajaram’s death.

nodes.title: Shahu
nodes.summary: Claimed the throne on release and built a court at Satara.

nodes.title: Sadāśivrāo Bhāu
nodes.summary: Commanded the Maratha expedition that reached Panipat.

nodes.title: Kṛṣṇa across three texts
nodes.summary: Follow the Yamunā, Mathurā and Dvārakā readings and compare their sources.

nodes.title: Kṛṣṇa’s birth and the Yamunā
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa appears to Devakī and Vasudeva. At night, Vasudeva carries the infant across the Yamunā to Nanda’s household and returns with Yaśodā’s daughter.

nodes.title: Nanda’s household celebrates
nodes.summary: Nanda rejoices at the arrival of a son and arranges ceremonies. The village joins the celebration before the narrative turns back to the threat posed by Kaṃsa.

nodes.title: The return to Mathurā
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma enter Mathurā. The confrontation plays out at a wrestling arena. Kṛṣṇa leaps onto Kaṃsa’s platform and kills the king.

nodes.title: A city in the sea
nodes.summary: With Mathurā under threat, Kṛṣṇa consults Balarāma. The account describes a fortified city in the sea and the transfer of his people there.

nodes.title: A reunion at Kurukṣetra
nodes.summary: The Bhāgavata describes a solar eclipse and pilgrimage to Samanta-pañcaka. People from different places gather, and Kṛṣṇa’s family meets the community he knew in childhood.

nodes.title: Kaṃsa’s death in the Harivaṃśa
nodes.summary: In the Harivaṃśa, the arena confrontation ends with Kaṃsa’s death and Kṛṣṇa greeting Vasudeva. Read this as an attributed account alongside the Bhāgavata version.

nodes.summary: Compare the observance rule and two lunar month labels.
